title: T5 close read: make every task text in, text out, then change one variable at a time
summary: T5 turns translation, classification, summarization, and even scoring into “text in, text out,” then systematically compares architecture, pre-training objective, data, fine-tuning method, and scale from a single baseline. We work through why span masking saves compute, summarize each controlled experiment, and flag a duplicated row in the paper.
ai_summary: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (Raffel et al., Google, JMLR 2020) casts every NLP task into a text-to-text format. It compares architecture, pre-training objective, data sets, fine-tuning and multi-task strategies, and scaling on an encoder-decoder baseline of about 220 million parameters, and releases the roughly 750GB cleaned web corpus C4. Conclusions: encoder-decoder plus a denoising objective works best; denoising variants differ little and should be chosen by compute cost; too much data repetition hurts; scaling up the model usually beats training longer. The largest model, 11B-parameter T5, set the state of the art on 18 of 24 tasks.
brief: Problem: Pre-training methods were proliferating, with objectives, data, architectures, and scale all changing at once, making it hard to tell which choices actually mattered.
Method: Cast every task into a text-to-text format, start from a unified baseline and change one factor at a time, and produce the cleaned C4 corpus.
Result: Encoder-decoder plus span-masking denoising wins; data should be large and clean; bigger models generally beat longer training; T5-11B reaches the best results on 18 tasks.
Limitations: Changing one factor at a time may miss interactions; translation tasks did not exceed the best prior results; Table 10 has a suspicious duplicated row.

paper.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
paper.authors: Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, Peter J. Liu

cover.headline: Close read of the original T5 paper
cover.highlight: Everything is text in, text out

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In October 2019, nine Google authors including Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, and Katherine Lee released this 67-page paper; it was published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR) in 2020. The model it introduces is **T5**, short for Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer.

Its starting point is pragmatic: after BERT and GPT in 2018, pre-training methods exploded, and every paper changed the objective, the data, the architecture, or the scale, making it hard to tell which change actually helped. The paper says its main purpose is **not to propose new methods** but to systematically compare existing approaches in one unified framework.

That unified framework is **“text-to-text”**: translation, summarization, question answering, classification, and even regression tasks like scoring are all written as “input text, output text.” For translation, the input is “translate English to German: That is good.” and the output is “Das ist gut.”; for a sentence acceptability judgment, the output is “acceptable” or “not acceptable.” This means every task can use **the same model, the same loss function, the same hyperparameters, and the same decoding procedure**.

Under this framework, the paper starts from a baseline, changes one factor at a time, and compares model architectures, pre-training objectives, pre-training data, fine-tuning methods, multi-task training, and scaling approaches. To support this, the authors also clean roughly 750GB of English web text into a corpus called **C4**. Finally, they combine the best choices and train a model with up to 11 billion parameters, achieving the best results of the time on 18 of 24 tasks.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Turn every NLP task into “text in, text out,” then change one variable at a time like a controlled experiment to systematically answer which pre-training choices matter. The answer: encoder-decoder + span-masking denoising + large, clean data + a bigger model.

callout.title: Three small concepts you need for this read
callout.text: If they’re new to you, that’s fine; these three are enough:
list: **Pre-training + fine-tuning**: first train on a huge amount of unlabeled text, then continue training on a small amount of labeled data for the specific task. See the GPT-1 and BERT close reads.
**Encoder-decoder**: the encoder reads the input, and the decoder writes the output one word at a time, connected by attention. See the Transformer close read.
**Masked language model**: mask some words in the input and have the model guess them. This is the objective BERT uses.

sections.h: Text-to-text: one format for every task

blocks.p: The paper’s approach: prepend a **task prefix** to the original input to tell the model what to do; the output is the answer as text.

fig.title: How different tasks become text in, text out
fig.subtitle: Examples from Figure 1 and Section 2.4 of the paper
rows: translate English to German: That is good.
cola sentence: The course is jumping well.
stsb sentence1: The rhino grazed on the grass. sentence2: A rhino is grazing in a field.
mnli premise: I hate pigeons. hypothesis: My feelings towards pigeons are filled with animosity.
summarize: state authorities dispatched emergency crews tuesday to survey the damage…
six people hospitalized after a storm in attala county.

list: **Regression tasks fit too**: STS-B asks for a score from 1 to 5 for a pair of sentences. The paper finds that scores are mostly labeled at 0.2 intervals, so it rounds each score to the nearest 0.2 and writes it as a string (for example, 2.57 becomes “2.6”), effectively turning the task into 21-class classification.

**What if the output is not one of the labels?** If a classification task emits a word that is not a label (the paper’s example is “hamburger”), it is always counted as wrong. The paper says their model never did this.
**The prefix wording doesn’t matter much**: the paper says changing the exact wording of the prefix has limited effect, so it did not study it separately.

blocks.p: The idea is not entirely new: earlier work cast all tasks as question answering, and GPT-2 used prompts to let a language model do tasks zero-shot (see the GPT-2 close read). T5 differs in that it allows each task to be fine-tuned separately and can handle generation tasks such as translation and summarization, where the answer set cannot be enumerated.

sections.h: The baseline: an encoder-decoder roughly the size of BERT-Base

blocks.p: Every controlled experiment starts from the same baseline, changes one factor, and keeps the rest fixed. The paper calls this a “coordinate ascent” style of exploration and acknowledges that it may miss interactions between factors.

list: **Architecture**: a standard encoder-decoder Transformer with 12 encoder layers and 12 decoder layers; each layer is roughly the size of BERT-Base, for about 220 million parameters total. Layer normalization is applied at the input of each sublayer (scaling only, no additive bias), followed by a residual connection. Position information uses simplified relative position embeddings: each attention head learns only 32 scalars, bucketed by the offset between query and key, with offsets beyond 128 tokens assigned to the same bucket.
**Vocabulary**: SentencePiece is used to segment text into 32,000 subwords. The tokenizer is trained on a mixture of 10 parts English and 1 part each German, French, and Romanian, for translation.

**Pre-training**: train on C4 for 2^{19} = 524,288 steps, with about 2^{16} tokens per batch, for a total of about 2^{35} (about 34 billion) tokens—roughly one quarter of BERT’s. It uses the Adafactor optimizer.
**Fine-tuning**: train on each task for 2^{18} = 262,144 steps and pick the checkpoint with the best validation score.
**Pre-training objective**: randomly mask 15% of tokens, replace each consecutive span of masked tokens with a “sentinel” symbol, and require the model to output only the masked parts.

fig.title: Baseline scores, and how much pre-training helps
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper, validation set. GLUE and SuperGLUE are average scores over subtasks; CNNDM is ROUGE-2 for summarization; SQuAD is exact match; translation is BLEU.
fig.note: Except for English-French translation, where there is enough training data that pre-training doesn’t help much, pre-training brings large gains on every task. The paper trains the baseline 10 times to estimate random variation and uses that to judge whether later differences are significant.

callout.title: An experimental habit worth copying
callout.text: Many papers report only a single result. T5 first trains the baseline 10 times, computes the standard deviation for each metric, and bolds any result within two standard deviations of the best score. The paper also cautions that small datasets such as CoLA, CB, and COPA fluctuate a lot—CB’s validation set has only 56 examples—so comparing models only by average GLUE or SuperGLUE scores can be misleading.

sections.h: Architecture: encoder-decoder, decoder-only, or prefix language model

blocks.p: Three architectures were popular at the time, differing mainly in the attention “mask”: who can see whom.

list: **Encoder-decoder**: in the encoder, each position can see the entire input (fully visible); the decoder can see only the parts already generated (causal mask) and can see the encoder output through cross-attention. This is the architecture of the original Transformer and of T5.

**Decoder-only language model**: a single Transformer stack concatenates the input and output into one sequence, applies a causal mask throughout, and predicts from left to right. The GPT series uses this. The downside is that each input position can see only words to its left, which makes it harder to “read” the input.

**Prefix language model**: still one stack, but the input portion uses a fully visible mask and only the output portion uses a causal mask. The paper notes that, for classification, this is very similar to BERT.

blocks.p: How to compare fairly? The paper points out that parameter count and compute cannot be aligned: an L-layer encoder plus L-layer decoder has about the parameters of a 2L-layer language model, but only the compute of an L-layer language model, because the encoder processes only the input and the decoder only the output, while each layer of a language model processes input plus output.

fig.title: Comparing five architectures
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 of the paper (partial). P is the parameter count of a 12-layer BERT-Base-sized stack; M is the compute of a 12+12-layer encoder-decoder.
fig.note: Encoder-decoder + denoising objective is best on all tasks. Sharing parameters barely hurts; halving the depth clearly hurts. The denoising objective always beats the left-to-right language model objective.

sections.h: Pre-training objectives: what to mask, how much, and how

blocks.p: This is the paper’s most detailed section. It uses the same sentence, “Thank you for inviting me to your party last week.”, to demonstrate various objectives:

fig.title: One sentence, different objectives, different inputs and outputs
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper. <M> is the shared masking symbol; <X>, <Y>, and <Z> are distinct sentinel symbols; the BERT-style objective also replaces some words with random words (here “apple”).
rows: me to your party last week .
Thank you <M> <M> me to your party apple week .
party me for your to . last fun you inviting week Thank
Thank you <X> me to your party <Y> week .
Thank you me to your party week .
<X> for inviting me <Y> your party last <Z>

blocks.p: The paper narrows things down in four steps:

list: **Big picture**: BERT-style denoising is best; the prefix language model is close on translation; deshuffling is clearly worst.

**Simplifying BERT**: removing the “replace with random word” step, or only predicting the masked parts (replace corrupted spans, drop corrupted tokens), performs about the same. Predicting only the masked parts produces much shorter target sequences, so training is faster.
**How much to mask**: the paper tries 10%, 15%, 25%, and 50%. The differences are small; only 50% is clearly worse on GLUE and SQuAD. So it keeps BERT’s 15%.

**Span masking**: instead of masking tokens independently, mask consecutive spans. With an average span length of 3, this is slightly better than per-token masking on most non-translation tasks, and the sequences are shorter, so training is faster.

fig.title: Back-of-the-envelope: why predicting only masked parts and span masking saves compute
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: a 500-token text with 15% masked. The span-masking example comes from Section 3.3.4 of the paper; the other lengths are computed here according to the paper’s rules, and the number of spans for per-token masking is an expected value.
rows: BERT-style: output the full original sentence
fig.note: With span masking, input = 500 - 75 + 25 sentinels; target = 75 + 25 sentinels + 1 end sentinel. The decoder’s attention cost grows with target length, so shrinking the target from 500 to about 100 makes pre-training far cheaper.

blocks.p: The paper sums up this section candidly: the most significant difference is only that “denoising beats language modeling and deshuffling.” The denoising variants differ little, so **choose mainly by compute cost**. It adds that continuing to fine-tune these objectives probably won’t yield much, and that it may be better to explore entirely different ways of using unlabeled data.

quiz.q: What pre-training objective did T5 ultimately use?
options: Predict the next word from left to right
Randomly mask 15% of tokens as consecutive spans of average length 3, replace each span with a sentinel, and output only the masked spans
Shuffle the sentence and reconstruct it
quiz.why: This “span masking” objective performs about as well as the other denoising variants, but has the shortest target sequence and trains fastest. The paper’s principle: when performance is equal, choose by compute cost.

sections.h: Data: C4, and how much “clean” and “on-target” matter

blocks.p: C4 comes from Common Crawl web text from April 2019. Common Crawl produces about 20TB of text per month, but much of it is menus, error messages, and duplicated content. The paper cleans it with a simple set of rules:

list: Keep only lines that end in a period, question mark, exclamation mark, or end quote.
Discard pages with fewer than 3 sentences, and keep only lines with at least 5 words.
Remove any page that contains a word on the bad-words list.
Remove lines containing “Javascript,” pages containing “lorem ipsum” placeholder text, and pages containing curly braces (likely code).
Remove Wikipedia-style citation markers and boilerplate privacy policies and cookie notices.
Keep only one copy of any repeated three-sentence span; use language detection to keep only pages classified as English with probability at least 0.99.

fig.title: What happens with different pre-training data
fig.subtitle: From Table 8 of the paper (partial), validation set.
fig.note: Uncleaned C4 is worst on every task. Task-matched data sometimes helps: Wikipedia + Books does better on SuperGLUE, almost entirely because of MultiRC, whose data mostly comes from novels.

blocks.p: **On-target data helps, but it shrinks the dataset.** For example, WebText-like data performs well, but it uses 12 times as much raw web text and ends up only about 1/40 the size of C4. Smaller data means more reuse—so what does that cost?

fig.title: Too many data repeats degrade results
fig.subtitle: From Table 9 of the paper (partial). Total training is fixed at 2^{35} tokens, using only the first N tokens of C4, so the data is repeated many times.
fig.note: Repeating 64 times matters little; repeating thousands of times clearly hurts. Training loss also drops substantially as the data shrinks, and the paper thinks the model is starting to memorize the data. So it recommends using large datasets when possible.

sections.h: Training strategy: how many parameters to fine-tune, and whether to use multi-task learning

blocks.p: **Is fine-tuning only part of the parameters enough?** The paper compares two parameter-saving methods: inserting small “adapter” layers after each feed-forward network and training only those, or gradually “unfreezing” layers from the top. Both underperform fine-tuning all parameters. The adapter pattern is that small tasks need only a small internal dimension, while large tasks such as translation need a large dimension.

fig.title: Fine-tuning only some parameters underperforms full fine-tuning
fig.subtitle: From Table 10 of the paper (partial). d is the adapter’s internal dimension.
fig.note: Note that the d = 2048 row is identical to d = 128: all seven metrics in Table 10 match exactly (only five are shown here), most likely a copy-paste error in the table. See “A few details worth noting” below.

blocks.p: **Multi-task training**. In the text-to-text framework, multi-task training means sampling from a mixture of all the datasets. The hard part is how much to sample from each task: if you sample in proportion to dataset size, large tasks crowd out small ones. The paper sets a per-dataset cap K and then samples proportionally, or uses a “temperature” to level out the proportions. The result: plain multi-task training underperforms “pre-training + separate fine-tuning,” but **pre-training on the multi-task mixture first and then fine-tuning each task separately** performs on par with the baseline.

fig.title: Ways of doing multi-task training
fig.subtitle: From Table 12 of the paper (partial), validation set.
rows: Pre-training on supervised tasks only + fine-tuning
fig.note: “Leave-one-out” means deliberately leaving a particular task out during pre-training and then fine-tuning on it, to simulate encountering a new task; it is only slightly worse, suggesting multi-task pre-training does not seriously interfere with new tasks. Pre-training on supervised data only, without unlabeled data, is clearly worse across the board except on translation.

sections.h: Scale: how to spend 4x more compute

blocks.p: The paper poses a very practical question: “If you suddenly had 4x the compute, how would you use it?” It compares training longer, increasing the batch size, making the model bigger, and ensembling multiple models.

fig.title: The same 4x compute budget, allocated different ways
fig.subtitle: From Table 13 of the paper (partial), validation set.
fig.note: All of these options help. Scaling up the model is generally better than just training longer; a 2x larger model trained for 2x as long is roughly comparable to a 4x larger model, so the two can complement each other. Ensembling is best on summarization and translation but barely helps on SuperGLUE.

blocks.p: The paper also notes the flip side of these choices: a larger model makes downstream fine-tuning and inference more expensive, whereas pre-training a smaller model longer can spread that cost over many downstream tasks.

sections.h: Putting it all together: T5’s final recipe and results

blocks.p: The final T5 combines these findings: the span-masking objective (average length 3, mask 15%); pre-training for 1 million steps with batches of 2^{11} sequences of length 512, for about 1 trillion tokens total, roughly 32x the baseline; pre-training first on the multi-task mixture, then fine-tuning each task individually; and beam search with width 4 for translation and summarization. The model comes in five sizes:

fig.title: Five T5 sizes and their results
fig.subtitle: From Section 3.7 and Table 14 of the paper (partial), test set (SQuAD on validation). “Previous best” is as of October 24, 2019.
fig.note: SuperGLUE rises from 84.6 to 88.9, close to the human score of 89.8. None of the translation tasks beat the previous best result; the paper attributes this partly to pre-training only on English, while the best translation systems used data augmentation such as back-translation.

list: **GLUE**: averages 90.3, clearly surpassing the previous best on reasoning tasks such as MNLI, RTE, and WNLI.

**SuperGLUE**: leads by a wide margin, but on two reading comprehension tasks it “exceeds human performance,” which the paper says may indicate that the metrics for these tasks favor machine output; on COPA and WSC humans score 100%, and the model is still far behind.

**SQuAD**: scores more than a point above the previous best, but is already past the estimated human level (82.30 exact match), so the paper doubts there is much value in continuing to push this leaderboard.
**Summarization**: reaches the best result, but only ROUGE-2 leads clearly; the paper also notes that a high ROUGE score does not mean the summaries are more coherent.

blocks.p: **How much do improvements beyond scale matter?** The paper runs one final experiment for this: train the baseline on 1 trillion tokens too (matching scale), then compare it with T5-Base, which adds span masking, multi-task pre-training, and other improvements. T5-Base is better on every task, showing that success is not just from scale.

list: **Table 10 has a duplicated row**: the results for adapter dimension d = 2048 are exactly the same as for d = 128, all seven numbers identical. According to the paper’s statement that “large tasks need a large dimension,” 2048 should have done better on translation, so this row was most likely copied by mistake.

**“Exponential decay” is not actually exponential**: Section 3.1.2 says the learning rate follows 1 / √max(n, k), “remains at 0.01 for the first 10^{4} steps, then decays exponentially.” But 1 / √n is a power-law decay, much slower than exponential: by this formula, it is about 0.0032 at step 100,000 and about 0.0014 at step 524,288.
**“3B” is actually about 2.8 billion**: the main text says the 3B variant has about 2.8 billion parameters, but the note in Table 14 says 3 billion.

**The tokenization terminology is a bit muddled**: the paper says it uses SentencePiece to encode text as WordPiece tokens, while also citing the BPE paper and Kudo’s subword regularization paper. These three are related but distinct methods (see the BPE subword tokenization close read).

**The conclusions have qualifiers**: “encoder-decoder is best” holds in the “pre-train then fine-tune per task” setting; all comparisons change only one factor at a time at baseline scale, and the paper itself acknowledges it may miss interactions between factors.
**Text-to-text became the default mental model**: today’s large models almost all work through a “text in, text out” interface, and prompting is a natural extension of T5’s task prefixes.
**C4 became a common pre-training dataset**: C4 makes up 15% of LLaMA’s pre-training data.

**The architecture debate had a different ending**: T5 concluded that encoder-decoder was best, but later large language models (GPT-3, LLaMA, etc.) mostly chose decoder-only architectures. One reason is that the objective changed: when models are no longer fine-tuned per task but instead complete tasks directly through prompting, a large left-to-right stack is simpler and easier to scale.

**A through-line to multi-task and instruction-based training**: T5 found that “multi-task pre-training + fine-tuning” is no worse than plain pre-training; later work such as FLAN trained on many tasks written as natural language instructions, enabling zero-shot performance on unseen tasks (see the site’s alignment and safety track).

blocks.p: The next stop on this route is **sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE)**: Noam Shazeer, T5’s second author, proposed it in 2017 as a way for a model to have a huge number of parameters while using only a small fraction of them on each call.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: In the text-to-text framework, how is a regression task like STS-B, which requires a score from 1 to 5, handled?
options: Use a different regression output layer
Round the score to the nearest 0.2, write it as a string for the model to output, effectively turning it into 21-class classification
quiz.why: This is both the cost and the cleverness of “everything is text”: numbers are written as text too. At test time, if the model outputs a string that is a number between 1 and 5, convert it back to a float; otherwise count it as wrong.

quiz.q: Why does the paper say pre-training objectives “should mainly be chosen by compute cost”?
options: Because the various denoising objectives perform about the same, but their target sequence lengths differ a lot, and shorter ones train faster
Because the language model objective is best
Because the BERT objective is too complex
quiz.why: Aside from “denoising beats language modeling and deshuffling,” the differences among the other variants are all near the noise level. Span masking outputs only the masked parts, cutting target length from 500 to about 100.

quiz.q: In the “4x more compute” experiment, which approach is generally best?
options: Make the model bigger (2x model for 2x time, or 4x model), which usually beats just training longer
quiz.why: Scaling up the model usually helps more than just training longer; a 2x model for 2x time and a 4x model are roughly comparable. Ensembling is strong on some tasks but nearly useless on SuperGLUE.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is the text-to-text framework? How are classification, regression, and translation each written as text?
What are the differences among encoder-decoder, decoder-only, and prefix language model? Why can’t parameter count and compute be aligned at the same time?
What is T5’s span-masking objective? Why does it save compute compared with the BERT-style objective?
How was C4 cleaned? What effects do cleaning, on-target data, and repetition have?
What were the results of fine-tuning only some parameters and of multi-task training, respectively?
With 4x more compute, how does the paper suggest spending it?
What are the shortcomings of T5’s final results?
